newsitem.title: USA: Johnson & Johnson to buy Biopsys Medical.
newsitem.headline: Johnson & Johnson to buy Biopsys Medical.

text.p: Johnson & Johnson said on Thursday it will acquire Biopsys Medical, a California maker of products for diagnosing breast cancer, in a stock swap valued at about $310 million.

Under the terms of deal, Johnson & Johnson will offer $27.55 worth of its stock for each Biopsis share, which rose $1 to $26.75 on Nasdaq at mid-afternoon. Johnson & Johnson fell 25 cents to $59.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The ratio for the share exchange will be based on the average price of Johnson & Johnson stock during a 20-day period prior to Biopsys' stockholders' approval of the deal.
With the purchase, Johnson & Johnson will acquire Biopsys' year-old "Mammotome" products for diagnosing breast cancer using a "minimally invasive" procedure.
In the outpatient procedure done under local anaesthetic, doctors use a thin hollow needle to obtain multiple tissue samples.
"This is a very important strategic advance for our worldwide minimally invasive surgery franchise," said William C. Weldon, Johnson & Johnson's group chairman.
The acquisition could assure Johnson & Johnson of a lucrative niche in the emerging market for minimally invasive breast biopsies, analysts said.
Eli Kammerman of Salomon Brothers said Johnson & Johnson, based in New Brunswick, N.J., is securing an early foothold in a technology destined for fast growth.
"It (Biopsys) has already been used in 58,000 procedures in a little over a year, but will be used in 300,000 to 400,000 within the next three years," he predicted.

Johnson & Johnson already has a significant market presence in minimally invasive surgery, "so this would be a nice complement and extension of its product line," added Merrill Lynch drug analyst Margo Vignola.
She estimates the Biopsys system is now generating about $20 million to $25 million in annual sales, making Johnson & Johnson's purchase price about 12 times sales.
"It's high from a price to sales basis," she said, but from a long-term standpoint, "it's a smart investment."

Kammerman said the merger would pit Johnson & Johnson head-to-head against U.S. Surgical Corp., which he said is the only other company with comparably sophisticated and proven technology for breast biopsies.

"It's going to be an intense marketing battle, but I think the Biopsys product will eventually get 40 percent of the potential market for all breast biopsies," said Kammerman, who estimates Biopsys now holds about 7 percent to 9 percent.
Prudential Securities drug analyst Charlene Lu said the Biopsys method has some advantages of being "cheaper and less invasive" than U.S. Surgical's rival device.

But because U.S. Surgical's technology removes a bigger core of tissue, she said it is preferred by some surgeons and radiologists and has the potential several years from now of being used to surgically remove tumours as well as to diagnose them.

Lu said that while Biopsis, based in Irvine, Calif., had sales of $10 million in the nine months ending March 31, its technology could claim a substantial portion of a market worth between $300 million to $400 million in the next five years.
"And it will have Johnson & Johnson's huge marketing power -- hundreds of sales people instead of the 12 people that Biopsys now has," she added.
"Johnson & Johnson is a huge company with over $20 billion in revenues so this won't have a huge impact, but it will add maybe a few pennies to earnings in future years," she said.

Analysts said the deal probably would have little, if any, effect on Johnson & Johnson's earnings this year, but would likely boost annual earnings as of next year as the Biopsys technology begins to capture market share.
The merger is subject to the approval of Biopsys Medical stockholders and antitrust regulators.
